question: When your foot 'falls asleep' after sitting cross-legged, most people blame the blood supply being cut off. But the main thing being squashed is something else. What is it?
topic: Pins and needles and limbs falling asleep

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone believes a sleeping foot means the blood supply was cut off. The real culprit is a squashed nerve that has stopped carrying messages, which recasts a lifelong experience.
extra.verification_notes: Sources agree the main cause of a limb 'falling asleep' is temporary nerve compression, not blood-supply loss; one NBC piece mentions a possible vascular contribution but that does not undermine the answer (https://www.sciencealert.com/here-s-what-happens-when-your-foot-falls-asleep).

explanation: Pressure on a nerve stops it sending signals, so the foot goes numb. The pins and needles are the nerve noisily coming back online once you move.

question: When you bang your 'funny bone', the tingling shoots down into your hand. Which finger usually feels it most?
topic: Pins and needles and limbs falling asleep
source_excerpt: The ulnar nerve provides sensation in your small finger and part of your ring finger.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has felt the zing but never noticed where it lands. Players can recall the sensation and work it out, then learn the 'bone' is actually a nerve.
extra.verification_notes: The funny bone is the ulnar nerve, which supplies the little finger and half of the ring finger, so the little finger is the standard answer (https://assh.org/handcare/blog/what-is-the-funny-bone).

explanation: The funny bone isn't a bone at all. It's the ulnar nerve, lying almost bare at the elbow, and that nerve supplies your little finger and half of your ring finger.
